name: Cicada 3301
title: The Internet Puzzle That Recruited Codebreakers, Then Vanished
claims: Cicada 3301 is the name for three sets of puzzles posted online under the name "3301" between 2012 and 2014 | 1
First puzzle started January 4, 2012 on 4chan and ran for nearly a month | 1
Second round began January 4, 2013; third round posted on Twitter January 4, 2014 | 1
The third puzzle remains unsolved | 1
A new clue was posted on Twitter on January 5, 2016 | 1
Last verified OpenPGP-signed message in April 2017, denying validity of any unsigned puzzle | 1
Puzzles focused on data security, cryptography, steganography and internet anonymity | 1
Called "the most elaborate and mysterious puzzle of the Internet age"; listed by The Washington Post among top 5 eeriest unsolved mysteries of the Internet | 1
Speculation includes NSA, CIA, MI6, Mossad, a "Masonic conspiracy", a cyber mercenary group | 1
Others have called it an alternate reality game, but no company or individual has tried to monetize it | 1
Stated purpose was to recruit "highly intelligent individuals"; ultimate purpose remains unknown | 1
Theories include a secret society aiming to improve cryptography, privacy and anonymity, or a cult or religion | 1
Several 2012 solvers said 3301 typically uses non-puzzle recruiting but created the puzzles to find people with cryptography and computer security skills | 1

2013 solvers were asked about support for information freedom, online privacy and freedom, and rejection of censorship; those who answered satisfactorily were invited to a private forum and told to devise and complete a project furthering the group's ideals | 1
One solver did not finish his work on a method of general decryption, and the website was removed | 1
Another 2013 winner documented her experience on a video channel and now facilitates community efforts on a Discord server; other solver communities remain on message boards and forums | 1
Clues included digital images with hidden information, a telephone message, websites, and paper signs with QR codes | 1
Puzzles referenced literature, poetry, art and music; Agrippa, the Mabinogion and The Book of the Law were used | 1
Each clue was signed by the same OpenPGP private key | 1
In 2012 Chilean investigative police (PDI) in Los Andes Province claimed Cicada 3301 was a hacker group engaged in illegal activities; Cicada responded with a PGP-signed denial | 1

In July 2015 a group calling itself "3301" hacked a database; Cicada issued a signed statement saying it was not associated and did not condone use of its name, number or symbolism; the hackers later confirmed they were not affiliated | 1
US Navy released a cryptographic challenge in 2014 based on the puzzles, called Project Architeuthis | 1
2015 Person of Interest episode "Nautilus" featured a similar worldwide cryptographic game with a nautilus shell; creator and producer said Cicada 3301 was the inspiration, with the quoted line | 1
2021 comedy-thriller film Dark Web: Cicada 3301 follows a hacker in the recruitment game evading the NSA | 1
A researcher in Brooklyn, procrastinating on a paper, found the message on 4chan's /b/ board on a Friday night in January | 2
4chan has no search function, no tagging, no formal archive; most posts expire or are deleted within hours; no registration required | 2
4chan drew more than 1 million unique visitors a day (at the time of the article) | 2
Some commenters suggested the message might be an NSA recruiting exercise; the researcher had read that the NSA was using 4chan to scout hackers | 2
A commenter suggested opening the image in WordPad; hidden text read "TIBERIVS CLAVDIVS CAESAR says" followed by garbled text | 2
Tiberius Claudius was the fourth Roman emperor; shifting back four letters (Caesar cipher) revealed a URL | 2
The page showed a plastic duck with the text "WOOPS just decoys this way. Looks like you can't guess how to get the message out." | 2
Words "guess" and "out" suggested OutGuess; running the image through it gave a link to a subreddit | 2
The subreddit page had Mayan numerals, garbled letters, and images labeled "welcome" and "problems?" | 2
Someone posted a link to an anonymous Mibbit chat room; the researcher found it creepy and said most trolls do not put in this much energy | 2
Book codes, King Arthur and the Holy Grail led to a message "call us on us tele phone number" | 2
The researcher received a private message "You're way ahead of the others" and an invitation to a private chat room; others doubted or insulted them | 2
Recording said "Very good. You have done well", three primes associated with the original image, 3301 is one, multiply all three and add .com | 2
The first image's pixel dimensions were 509 and 503, both prime | 2

The resulting site showed a cicada image above a three-day countdown; OutGuess revealed "You have done well to come this far. Patience is a virtue. Check back at 17:00 on Monday, 9 January 2012. UTC." | 2
It was 2 a.m. when the researcher reached the next level | 2

sources.title: Chasing the Cicada: Exploring the Darkest Corridors of the Internet | Mental Floss
